title: Show HN: Europe Instead – find the European version of the tools you use
summary: Hi HN, I'm Rafael. Europe Instead is a directory of European-made software: https://europeinstead.com I built it because every time we needed a new tool at my startup, Upgrid, I ended up doing the same research again: who actually owns this company, where is the data hosted, who are the subprocessors. After doing that enough times I got tired of it and started writing it down properly. The existing "EU alternatives" lists didn't help much, because most check one thing, the legal seat. A company registered in Berlin can be owned by a US parent, run on AWS us-east-1, and send your data to a dozen US subprocessors. That is a different risk from a Berlin company on Hetzner. So every tool gets two separate answers: - Origin score (0-100): how European the company is, from five parts: legal entity, ownership and control, operations, data residency, and openness. Weights are published on the method page. - Exposure level (1-5): which jurisdictions can legally reach the core customer data, based on where it is hosted and who the subprocessors are. Every fact links to the page it came from, with the check date and usually a quoted line. If we couldn't find evidence, the fact is shown as "not verified" and scores zero, rather than being guessed. Right now that is about a quarter of all facts, which tells you something about how little vendors disclose. Some details: - 1,818 tools from 33 countries, across 212 categories, mapped as alternatives to 453 US products (Calendly, Typeform, Intercom, Google Analytics, and so on). - Vendors can correct their record by form or email. Corrections are reviewed by a person and logged in a public change history. - Listing is free and unconditional. No backlink required, and rankings can't be bought. If I ever sell sponsored slots, they sit above the ranked list with their own numbering and a "Sponsored" label; the ranking below always starts at 1 and doesn't move. A few things you might find useful: - "Alternative to X" pages: name the tool you use today and see the European ones that do the same job. - Stacks: a full European set of tools for a small company, one per job. - A read-only API and an MCP server, so you can ask an AI assistant for a European alternative and get the sourced record back ( https://europeinstead.com/developers ). - A free badge vendors can embed. It links to their live record and has no tracking. What I'd like from you: tell me where the data is wrong, and tell me where the method is wrong. In particular I'm unsure how to treat the UK and Switzerland (included, country always shown so you can apply a stricter definition), and whether "uses AWS Frankfurt" should count against a tool as much as it does now. title: Show HN: Mobile-friendly image editor inspired by GIMP (layers, selection, etc)
summary: I don't know if anyone else is still out here crafting memes by hand... but I do! And I find the capabilities of frontier models jarringly bad with this regard. Also... memes are supposed to be made with love! Since I don't always have access to my laptop, I want to be able to do real image editing on my phone. You know.. selection, layering, filters, etc. No OS image editor comes close to this and commercial ones are expensive or cluttered with ads. So I designed a mobile-friendly layout and tasked Claude to port over all of the GIMP tools to this mobile application. It also has some convenience features (AI object selection, tool lookup via BM25), but the core edit loop is similar to GIMP. The filters are the original GIMP filters but almost entirely ported to GPU! So I found it actually very responsive and usable on my potato phone even working on 12MP pictures. I found it fun to play with it and its finally on Google Play now! Let me know what you think :) Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50664650 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

title: Show HN: Scolast – AI tutor for autodidacts inspired by Bloom's 2 sigma problem
summary: I was using Claude to learn physics and I was getting a bit frustrated with the interface (I kept interrupting the conversation to get a quick explainer on something, and there was no good interface for Claude to ask me questions) so I built Scolast! It's an AI tutor that follows Bloom's findings ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloom%27s_2_sigma_problem ) that 1 to 1 tutoring, using mastery learning (basically only moving ahead when the student has demonstrated they learned something, but also moving ahead as quickly as possible) can have pretty incredible results, around two standard deviations higher than regular classroom learning. Bloom called it a problem because this was obviously untenable - but it's actually possible now! I also added little side explainers for anything that's confusing, plus worksheets, and I've been iterating on the voice of the tutor, to try to get a sort of Feynman-y focus on the whys and the experiments and experiences that motivated each piece of knowledge. I find that it's quite remarkable, I'm actually retaining some of the physics I've never been able to retain in the past, and it seems useful in a lot of other domains - my wife used it for language learning and to pass a yoga exam; I've used it to learn some machine learning subjects, etc. One interesting side effect is that I find using it quite tiring, and I actually use tokens very slowly compared to agentic coding - when you actually have to read every token carefully you really get your money's worth. Would love to get people's thoughts so I'm throwing in $3 in free tokens while my budget lasts. After that you can buy tokens and I'm charging an extra 10% to cover everything else. Eventually I'd like to hook it up to people's existing subscriptions, I've applied to OAI's program for this, waiting to see if Ant will offer it. Cheers Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50661473 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

title: Show HN: Blur – a Mac app that hides secrets during screen sharing
summary: Hi HN! We built Blur for a moment you’ll recognize. You’re sharing screen on the call and open some app or file to show something, and accidentally discover that you also demo your API tokens. Blur detects credentials as they appear and blurs just that part of the screen. The rest stays readable, so you can keep walking someone through the file. You can also hide entire apps from the screen share. Detection runs entirely on your Mac. We use CoreML to run MobileNetV4 on Apple’s Neural Engine. Your screen content stays on your machine. Blur doesn’t ask for a username, an ID, or any other personal information. It only connects to the network to check for app updates. There is optional support for Jev-like networks, but it is disabled by default. If you try it, we’d love to hear how it works for you.
